# Data

## What this repository actually trains on
**Everything reported in this repo uses a synthetic proxy dataset generated by `src/directed_speech_detector/data/synthetic.py`.** It is not real speech and not real voice-assistant traffic. No external dataset was downloaded (Hugging Face and dataset hosts were unreachable from the build sandbox; see `DECISIONS.md` D1).

| Split | Utterances | Households | Seed offset |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| train | 6,000 | 240 | data seed + 0 |
| val | 1,000 | 40 | data seed + 1,000,003 |
| test | 2,000 | 80 | data seed + 2,000,003 |

Splits are household-disjoint: the enrolled voice, family voices and enrollment clip of a test household never appear in training. Class prior is ~50% directed. Generation is deterministic per (split seed, household) and independent of worker count (`tests/test_synthetic.py`).

## Generator summary
- **Audio**: 16 kHz, ≤ 4 s. Syllable-timed additive-harmonic synthesis with vowel formants, speaker pitch/vocal-tract scaling, breathiness, onset noise bursts; synthetic reverberation (RT60 0.1–0.9 s); pink or babble noise at SNR −2…30 dB.
- **Transcript**: slot-filled templates (51 sentence patterns). Some command-like sentences are valid in both classes (identical strings), so text alone is ambiguous by design. ASR-style word deletions/substitutions whose rate rises as SNR falls (2% at ≥ 16 dB up to 20% at ≤ 0 dB).
- **Class priors built in (assumptions, not measurements)**: directed speech has mean SNR 16 dB vs 10 dB, mean RT60 0.25 s vs 0.45 s, level −24 vs −30 dBFS, speaking-rate 0.95 vs 1.10, pitch-depth 0.18 vs 0.10; directed is spoken by the enrolled user 88% of the time vs 35% for background.
- **Enrollment**: one clean-ish clip (≤ 4 s) per household, reduced to a 80-dimensional mean/std log-mel profile.

## Caveats (read before quoting any number)
1. Cues are separable *by construction*; good scores show the pipeline can exploit multimodal evidence, not that the task is solved on real data.
2. The acoustic differences between classes are simplistic stand-ins for real device-directed cues (prosody, proximity, gaze, dialogue context).
3. Templates are English-only, 218-word lexicon; real ASR errors are far more varied.
4. The speaker cue relies on synthetic voices whose parameters are random draws, which is easier than real speaker verification.

## Public datasets for the full run (not downloaded; licences **not verified** from this sandbox)
| Dataset | Intended use | Licence note (verify on the dataset page) |
|---|---|---|
| SLURP | directed (assistant-style commands) | annotations CC BY 4.0; audio terms may be non-commercial |
| Fluent Speech Commands | directed | custom research licence |
| LibriSpeech | background (read speech) | CC BY 4.0 |
| AMI Meeting Corpus | background (multi-party conversation) | CC BY 4.0 |
| Common Voice | background | CC0 |

Even with these, the "directed vs background" labels are a **proxy**: SLURP/FSC are users *deliberately* talking to a mock assistant in clean conditions, and LibriSpeech/AMI are read or conversational speech. The label is partly dataset identity (a shortcut), so results must be interpreted with that confound in mind. The real-audio entry point is `data/manifest.py` (CSV of WAVs); see `notebooks/colab_full_training.ipynb`.
